passage: I asked for eleven o'clock. Mummy and Papa said nine-thirty. My first reaction was a hot flush and a list of arguments ready in my throat, mostly about how Mridul's parents let him stay till midnight. But halfway through, I noticed Papa's face. The rule had been seven, and he had already moved to nine-thirty. That was a real step. So I said, "Okay, nine-thirty. Can we look at it again at Diwali?" Mummy wrote the date on the fridge calendar. Mridul thought I was mad. "Just push, they'll cave," he said. Maybe. But by December I had ten, and by February ten-thirty, each time because I had kept my word on the last one. Mridul is still fighting for midnight. I'm Saurabh, and I stopped counting it as losing.

qa.q: What hour did Mummy and Papa agree to at first?
What did Saurabh feel at the start, and what changed it?
qa.a: Saurabh felt a hot flush and an urge to argue, but noticing that Papa had already moved from seven to nine-thirty changed it into acceptance of a real step.

qa.q: What could Saurabh do if the review date brings another refusal, and why?
qa.a: Saurabh could point to the weeks of on-time returns and ask for a smaller step, because steady gains tend to expand privileges more than an all-or-nothing push.

qa.q: How might Mridul see Saurabh's choice to accept nine-thirty?
qa.a: Mridul thinks Saurabh is mad to accept less and believes pushing will make parents cave, though Mridul is still fighting for midnight.

grounding: Parents agree to an earlier hour than requested, and the teen accepts it, sets a review date and notes that gradual gains kept steadily expand privileges more than an all-or-nothing demand.
